transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, hi. Thank you for fitting me in. I, um... I came in because things have just been feeling really off lately, and I finally decided I should probably talk to someone. I've been teaching for a long time, and I've always prided myself on being incredibly organized, but ever since the district put this massive bilingual social-emotional learning rollout on my plate—which, by the way, they did right on top of my regular teaching schedule without any extra prep periods—I just haven't been myself. 

I mean, it's a wonderful initiative in theory, you know? The kids really do need that emotional support, especially in two languages, and I completely support the philosophy behind it. But the execution has just been dumped entirely on us with barely any guidance. I still get through the day, of course. I show up, I teach my classes, I get it done because that's what you do. But internally... I just feel so wound up all the time. And discouraged, I guess. In a way that really, truly isn't like me at all. I’m usually the one on top of everything, the one other teachers come to for advice on structuring their week, but lately? I’ve started putting off my lesson plans. 

And the emails! The emails just pile up from parents and administration, and I find myself ignoring messages I used to handle without a second thought. I used to just sit down, clear out my inbox, and have my plans ready for the next day before I even left the building. Now I just look at the computer screen and think, I just can't do this right now, and then I keep putting it off until the very last possible second. It's just so frustrating because I know how to do my job, but this one extra rollout has just completely thrown off my whole system, and I just can't seem to shake this feeling...
Do you feel anxious most of the time?

Well, I don't know if "anxious" is really the right word for it, at least not in the way I usually hear people use it. When I think of being anxious most of the time, I picture someone who can't sit still, or who is constantly worrying about every little thing in their life, you know, like what if the car breaks down or what if someone gets sick. And that’s really not me at all. 

I mean, sure, I have moments during the day where I look at the clock and realize I have exactly four minutes to transition my fifth graders from math centers to the new SEL curriculum, and I haven't even pulled up the Spanish vocabulary slides yet because the Wi-Fi in my wing of the building is always spotty. In those moments, yes, I feel a spike of stress. But it's not this constant, all-day anxiety. It's more of a... a heavy, dragging feeling? Like I'm just wading through mud. 

I'm not sitting at my desk trembling or having racing thoughts about the future. I'm just sitting there staring at the screen, feeling completely drained and, frankly, just annoyed that I can't seem to muster the energy to care about the emails the way I used to. So, no, I wouldn't say I'm walking around feeling anxious all day long. I'm still functioning, I'm still teaching my lessons, I'm just... stuck. Does that make sense? Because I really want to be clear that I'm not a nervous wreck, I'm just incredibly frustrated by how this one administrative decision has completely derailed my usual workflow, and it's leaving me feeling so unmotivated instead of panicked.
Do you feel sad most of the time?

No, I wouldn't say "sad" is the right word either. I mean, when I think of being sad, I think of crying, or grieving, or just feeling this deep sorrow, you know? Like when my dog passed away a few years ago, or when I watch one of those heartbreaking documentaries on PBS. That’s sadness. This isn't that. I'm not sitting in my classroom crying at my desk after the kids leave. 

It's really more of a profound sense of exhaustion and... just feeling overwhelmed and depleted. Like I said, I've always been the kind of teacher who leaves at the end of the day feeling a sense of accomplishment. I'd have my colored folders all lined up, my whiteboard prepped for the next morning, and I'd walk out to my car feeling good about what we achieved. Now, I walk out to my car and I just feel heavy. But it's not sadness. It's just this incredibly frustrating lack of drive. 

I actually had a moment just last Thursday—or was it Wednesday? No, Thursday, because it was right after the staff meeting where they introduced yet another logging system for the SEL modules. I came home, sat on the couch, and my husband asked how my day was, and I just stared at him. I didn't want to cry, I didn't feel tearful, I just felt entirely drained of any enthusiasm for a job I've loved for twenty-five years. So, no, I'm not walking around feeling sorrowful or weeping. It's just this persistent, annoying feeling of being stuck in the mud and not having the energy to pull myself out of it, all because of this one massive, poorly rolled-out initiative. It's just draining, not sad.
Do you find yourself enjoying the things you used to like doing?

Well, that's an interesting question. I mean, I suppose I still enjoy things, but it's... it's just different right now. Like, take my gardening, for example. I have always loved my garden. I have these beautiful raised beds in the backyard—tomatoes, zucchini, a whole herb section with basil and cilantro that I use for cooking. Usually, on a Saturday morning, I'd be out there by 8:00 AM, coffee in hand, pulling weeds, checking on the soil moisture, just really taking my time and enjoying the peace and quiet before the weekend really gets going. It's always been my way to decompress after a long week of teaching. 

But lately? Since this whole SEL rollout started taking over my life? I look out the kitchen window at the garden, and I know the tomatoes need staking, and I know I should be out there, but I just... I don't go. Or if I do go out, I'm just rushing through it. I'll quickly water everything, maybe pull one or two obvious weeds, and then I just go back inside. It's not that I don't like gardening anymore—I still love the idea of it, and I still love having fresh vegetables—but the actual act of doing it just feels like another chore on my list instead of a hobby I enjoy. 

And it's the same with reading. I've been in this book club with a few other teachers and some neighborhood friends for, gosh, it must be going on twelve years now. We meet once a month, we drink wine, we talk about the book—or sometimes we just talk about our lives, you know how book clubs are. I'm usually the one who finishes the book a week early and comes with discussion questions. But the last two books? I haven't even made it past the third chapter. I sit down on the couch in the evening, open the book, read the same paragraph four times because my mind is wandering back to my lesson plans and whether I logged the emotional check-ins correctly on the new district portal, and then I just close the book and turn on the TV instead. 

So, I wouldn't say I've completely lost the ability to enjoy things. I still like the idea of my hobbies, and I still enjoy spending time with my husband and my friends. It's just that the energy required to actually engage in those things, to really sink into them and get that sense of joy and relaxation I used to get... it's just not there right now. It's like this whole work situation has just sapped my bandwidth for everything else. Does that make sense? I'm not sitting around hating everything, I just can't seem to muster the enthusiasm to actually do the things I know I like.
Have you noticed any changes in your sleep lately?

Well, actually, no. It’s funny you ask that, because you would think, with all this frustration about the new SEL curriculum and the logging portal, that I’d be lying awake at two in the morning staring at the ceiling, right? I know some of the other teachers in my wing—like Sarah, who teaches sixth-grade science, she was just telling me in the breakroom on Tuesday that she hasn't slept a full night since October because she's so stressed about the new evaluation metrics. But for me, it's really not like that at all. 

I’ve been sleeping pretty much the exact same way I always do. My husband, Tom, he has terrible sleep apnea, so I know what bad sleep looks like. He’s up and down, adjusting his mask, but I just sleep right through it. By the time nine-thirty or ten o'clock rolls around, I am just so mentally and physically done for the day. I’ll do my nighttime routine, wash my face, put on my moisturizer, maybe try to read—though, like I said earlier, I usually just end up watching an episode of Jeopardy or something mindless—and once my head hits the pillow, I am out. 

I sleep straight through until my alarm goes off at 5:45 AM. I'm not tossing and turning, I'm not waking up in a cold sweat panicking about lesson plans, none of that. If anything, because I feel so heavy and drained all day long, sleep is the one thing that actually comes easily right now. It's just that when the alarm does go off, I wake up and I still have that same dragging, unmotivated feeling waiting for me. But the actual hours I'm asleep? No, those haven't changed a bit. I'm getting my solid seven to eight hours every single night.
Are you avoiding certain tasks or situations at work because you feel overwhelmed or drained?

Well, I wouldn't say I'm outright avoiding things, like hiding in the staff lounge or anything dramatic like that. I mean, I'm still in the classroom every day. I'm still teaching my kids, still doing my morning bus duty, still meeting all my basic responsibilities. I would never just abandon my students or leave them hanging, you know? That's just not who I am, not after twenty-five years in this district. 

But... I will admit that things are slipping in a way they never, ever used to. It’s exactly that feeling of being drained that I was just talking about. Because I just don't have that extra mental energy right now, I’ve found myself missing or pushing back planning deadlines. Like, just last week, the grade-level team needed our math pacing guides for the upcoming quarter. Normally, I’m the first one to have that uploaded to the shared district drive. I usually do it a week early! I like to have it done and out of the way. But this time? Friday afternoon came and went, and I just... I hadn't done it. I kept opening the document on my laptop during my planning period, looking at the empty grid, thinking, "I just cannot look at another spreadsheet right now," and then I'd just minimize the window. 

It actually got to the point where Linda—she teaches the other fifth-grade section across the hall from me—she had to pop her head into my room on Monday morning and gently remind me that the principal needed them by noon. And honestly, it was so embarrassing. I have never been the teacher who needs a reminder for something as basic as a pacing guide. I’ve always been the reliable one! I'm usually the one who reminds the younger teachers about our deadlines. But lately, I’ve had to have Linda or the front office secretary nudge me about things I used to do on autopilot, like turning in the weekly newsletter draft or even just submitting my afternoon attendance on time. 

So, I'm still doing the core of my job—the actual teaching part, standing in front of the room with the kids—but all the administrative stuff, the planning, the paperwork... I'm just dragging my feet on it. I guess you could call that avoiding, in a way, just because I'm so overwhelmed by the sheer volume of it all now, especially with that new SEL logging system hanging over my head on top of everything else. I just keep putting off the things that require that extra executive function until someone literally taps me on the shoulder and says, "Hey, we need this." It's just so unlike me.
Do you find yourself feeling irritable more often than usual?

Irritable? You know, no, I really don't think so. I mean, you would probably expect me to be snapping at people, especially with how overwhelming this whole new curriculum rollout has been, but I really haven't been. Even with the kids—and let me tell you, fifth graders have a way of testing your patience, even on a good day. Just yesterday, for instance, we were doing a fractions review, and I had three different students ask me where to put their names on the worksheet, even though it's the exact same format we've been using since August. A lot of teachers, especially the newer ones, might get a little short with them over something like that. But I just... I don't. I just take a breath, point to the top right corner, and move on. 

And it's the same thing at home with my husband, Tom. He's a wonderful man, but he has this habit of leaving every single kitchen cabinet door open when he goes in there to make a sandwich. It used to drive me absolutely up the wall! I'd always be following right behind him, shutting them all and making little sarcastic comments about whether we live in a barn. But lately? I don't even have the energy to be annoyed by it. I just walk right past the open cabinets. 

I see some of the other teachers getting really snappy in the staff room, complaining loudly about the administration, slamming the microwave door when someone leaves their time on the clock... but I just sit there with my tea. I don't feel angry or short-tempered at all. If anything, I just feel sort of numb to the little annoyances that might normally get under my skin. It's like I don't even have the spare emotional bandwidth required to get mad or irritable right now. I just want to get through the day, you know? So no, I wouldn't say I'm irritable. Just... deflated, I guess.
Do you feel like you've lost interest in things you normally enjoy?

Lost interest? No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. I mean... I still very much enjoy my hobbies. Like, take my garden, for example. I have these raised beds in the backyard that my husband, Tom, built for me a few years ago. I always do heirloom tomatoes, zucchini, some bell peppers, and a whole row of marigolds to keep the bugs away. And I still absolutely love going out there. Just this past Sunday, the weather was finally nice enough, and I spent a good two hours out there with my trowel, turning the soil and getting things prepped for spring. I still get that exact same little thrill when I'm out there in the dirt, you know? 

And my book club, too. We meet on the second Thursday of every month—well, usually the second Thursday, unless there's a holiday or something—at this little café just down the street from the school. We're reading this historical fiction novel right now. It's set in 1940s London, which, honestly, usually isn't my favorite era because those stories can get so heavy, but the author's writing is just beautiful. And I still really look forward to going. I still make sure I read the chapters, I still enjoy sitting there with the ladies, having my decaf coffee, and just debating the characters' choices. 

So, no, the interest is definitely still there. Like I was saying earlier, I might be completely physically and mentally drained when I get home from school, and I might just want to zone out in front of the TV on a Tuesday night because I don't have the brainpower for anything else. But on the weekends? If Tom says, "Hey, let's go check out that antique mall over in the next county," I still jump at the chance. I still love looking at the old depression glass and the vintage schoolhouse items. It's not like the color has drained out of my world or anything dramatic like that. I still love the things I love. The personal side of my life, my interests... those haven't changed. It's just the work stuff that's dragging me down. But my hobbies? No, I still enjoy them just as much as I always have.
Are there any specific work-related tasks that you've been putting off or trying to avoid lately?

Well, yes, exactly like I was saying earlier with the pacing guides, it’s really the administrative and planning side of things that is taking the hit. I mean, I came in to see you in the first place because ever since the district put this massive new bilingual social-emotional learning rollout on my plate—which, by the way, they did right in the middle of the semester, on top of my regular teaching load—I just haven't been myself. 

I still get through the day, obviously. I'm there for the kids. But I just feel so wound up and discouraged in a way that really isn't like me at all. And because of that, the specific things I'm avoiding are mostly my lesson plans and my emails. 

And I mean, these are things I used to handle without a second thought! I used to pride myself on my inbox. I was the teacher who cleared out every single message before packing up my tote bag at 3:30. A parent asking about a field trip permission slip? Answered. The principal sending out a memo about the fire drill schedule? Read and filed. But lately, I look at that little red notification bubble on my screen climbing up to thirty, forty, fifty unread messages, and I just physically cannot bring myself to click on them. I just minimize the browser. 

And the lesson plans... oh, it breaks my heart a little, honestly. I used to actually enjoy doing my lesson plans. I would sit down on a Thursday afternoon with my colored flair pens and my planner, and I'd map out the whole next week. It was satisfying! But now, having to figure out how to integrate all these new bilingual SEL modules into the reading and social studies blocks we already barely have time for... I just freeze. I'll take my planner out, look at the blank week, feel my chest get all tight and wound up, and I just push it to the side of my desk. I've been waiting until Sunday night, or even Monday morning, and just sort of cobbling things together at the last minute or recycling old materials from three years ago. It's just so discouraging to see myself operating this way when I know how on top of things I usually am.
Have you been having trouble concentrating on things lately?

Concentrating? Hmm... no, I really don't think so. I mean, you might assume that with how much I’ve been avoiding my emails and the lesson planning like I just mentioned, that my brain is just scattered, but it’s really not a focus issue at all. When I actually sit down to do a task, I can lock right in just fine. 

Like, for example, grading the fifth graders' state capital projects this past weekend. They had to build these little shoebox dioramas and write a three-page report, which, let me tell you, for an eleven-year-old, three pages is like asking them to write a doctoral dissertation. I sat at my dining room table on Saturday morning—Tom was out at the hardware store because the latch on our side gate has been sticking again—and I spent a solid three and a half hours going through those reports with my grading rubric. I didn't lose my place, I wasn't getting distracted by the television or checking my phone every five minutes. I was completely zeroed in on making sure I was giving them fair, detailed feedback on their grammar and their historical accuracy. 

And it's the same thing with that book club I mentioned earlier. That historical fiction novel set in 1940s London? It has multiple timelines jumping back and forth between the Blitz and the late twenties, and there are about a dozen different characters whose names all sound incredibly similar—lots of Edwards and Edmunds and Eleanors. If my concentration were slipping, I would be completely lost trying to keep all those family trees and shifting perspectives straight. But I follow it perfectly fine. I can read for an hour before bed and remember exactly what happened the next day without having to flip back and reread pages. 

So, no, my actual ability to focus and concentrate? That's perfectly intact. It's really just the emotional energy to tackle the new bilingual curriculum that's completely shot. If I need to focus on something routine, or something I actually want to do, my brain works just as well as it always has.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite lately?

Appetite? Oh, no. No, my appetite hasn't changed a bit. I know some people, when they get stressed out, their stomach just ties itself in knots and they can't eat a thing. My sister is like that—she drops five pounds the minute things get even a little bit hectic at her job. But I’ve never been that way, and I'm certainly not now. I still eat like clockwork. 

Tom and I always sit down for breakfast around 6:15 every morning. I usually make a bowl of steel-cut oats with some walnuts and a little drizzle of maple syrup, and I still finish every single bite. It just holds me over so much better than cold cereal when I'm on my feet in front of the kids all morning. And for lunch, I always pack my own bag. I honestly can't stomach the cafeteria food—you really wouldn't believe what they try to pass off as a hot meal these days, it's just criminal—so I usually bring a nice spinach salad or whatever leftovers we have from the night before. Just yesterday I brought a big container of the turkey chili I made in the slow cooker over the weekend, and I ate the whole thing in the teachers' lounge while I was, well, aggressively ignoring my email inbox like I told you about. 

And dinner is exactly the same as always, too. Tom loves to grill, so even though it's been a little brisk in the evenings, he was out there last night doing chicken breasts, and we had that with some roasted sweet potatoes and green beans. So, no, I'm definitely still eating just fine. I haven't lost my taste for food, and I haven't started stress-eating a bunch of junk food either. The overwhelming feelings are really just affecting my work and my lesson planning, but my stomach is completely normal.
Do you feel less confident in your abilities as a teacher lately?

Confidence? Oh, no, absolutely not. I mean, I know I've been talking your ear off about how much I'm struggling with this new bilingual social-emotional learning curriculum, and how I'm avoiding my emails and letting my lesson planning slide until Sunday night, but none of that is because I doubt my actual teaching abilities. Not for a second. 

I've been in the classroom for... gosh, it'll be twenty-eight years this coming fall. Twenty-eight years! I started right out of my master's program. You don't do something for nearly three decades without knowing exactly what you're capable of. I know how to run a classroom. I know how to manage twenty-five ten-year-olds who all want to talk at the same time, and I know how to break down long division so that the kid who has been struggling all year finally gets that "aha" moment. I know how to talk to parents when their child is acting out without making them feel defensive. Those are my core skills, and they haven't gone anywhere. 

Just the other day, actually, we were doing a unit on the water cycle, and the lesson I had planned—which, yes, I threw together at the last minute because of all this stress—was just not landing. The kids were getting restless, eyes were glazing over. Ten years ago, I might have panicked. But now? I just pivoted. I stopped the lesson, had everyone get up, and we did this whole interactive, kinesthetic activity where they had to act out evaporation and condensation. It was loud, it was a little chaotic, but by the end of it, they completely understood the concepts. You can't do that if you don't have confidence in your abilities.

So, no, I know I'm a good teacher. A great teacher, really. The problem isn't my confidence in my skills. The problem is that the district keeps piling on these massive, top-down initiatives—like this bilingual SEL rollout—without giving us the time, the resources, or the training to actually implement them properly. It's the sheer volume of the administrative burden that has me feeling so wound up and discouraged, not any doubt about my own competence. If they just let me teach, I'd be perfectly fine. But they want me to be a data analyst, a social worker, a bilingual curriculum specialist, and an administrator all at once, and that's what's burning me out. But my actual teaching? No, I'm as confident in that as I've ever been.
Have you noticed any changes in your physical health lately?

Physical health? Oh, goodness, no. No, my physical health is perfectly fine. I mean, you would probably think with all the stress I’ve been under with this ridiculous new curriculum rollout, that I’d be getting headaches or, I don't know, catching every single cold the kids bring into the classroom. And let me tell you, fifth graders are basically walking petri dishes, especially right around this time of year when the weather can't make up its mind. Half my class has been coughing for a month straight. But I haven't had so much as the sniffles. 

I actually just had my annual physical with my primary care doctor, Dr. Henderson, back in... oh, it must have been late February, right before the district dropped all this new administrative paperwork on us. And everything was absolutely pristine. My blood pressure is right where it should be—which is honestly a minor miracle considering what I have to deal with at work—and my cholesterol is fantastic, probably because I’m so diligent about packing those healthy lunches I told you about. 

And I still make sure to stay active, too. Teaching keeps you on your feet all day, of course, but beyond that, Tom and I always take our dog for a walk every single evening. We have a golden retriever mix named Barnaby, he's about six years old now, and he just has to get his energy out. So after we finish dinner and clean up the kitchen, we take him on this big loop around our subdivision. It takes about forty-five minutes, and we walk past the neighborhood park and down around the cul-de-sac... and I haven't missed a single night of that. Even when I’m dreading going into work the next day, I still get my walking shoes on. 

So, physically? I feel just as healthy and capable as I did ten years ago. No strange aches or pains, no fatigue during the day, nothing like that. My body is holding up beautifully. It really is just this mental and emotional exhaustion from the sheer volume of work they expect us to do without any support. But physically, no, I'm doing just fine.
Are you feeling pleasure or enjoyment from activities that you normally find pleasurable?

Pleasure? Oh, yes, absolutely. I haven't lost my joy for life or anything like that. I know sometimes when people get overwhelmed they just want to pull the covers up over their heads and sleep all weekend, but that is certainly not me. I still absolutely love my weekends and my hobbies. 

For instance, my garden. I have this perennial border along the back fence that I’ve been cultivating for... gosh, it must be five or six years now. And I still get just as much satisfaction out of it as I always have. Just this past Saturday, the weather was finally cooperating, so I spent a good three hours out there. The hostas are coming in beautifully this year, and I had to divide some of the daylilies—because if you don't stay on top of those, they will just completely take over the bed, they're practically weeds if you let them go—and I was just as happy as a clam with my gardening gloves on and my hands in the dirt. 

And Tom and I still have our Sunday morning routine, too. We always get the Sunday paper—the actual physical paper delivered to the driveway, which I know makes us absolute dinosaurs, but I just cannot do the crossword puzzle on an iPad, it is simply not the same without a real pen in your hand. We sit out on the sunporch with our coffee, and we tackle it together. He usually handles the sports and geography clues, and I do the literature and history ones. It’s honestly my favorite part of the week, and I still look forward to it just as much as I ever did. 

So, no, I'm definitely still enjoying the things I love. I still enjoy my garden, I still love taking Barnaby on those evening walks I mentioned, I still love reading my historical fiction novels before bed. It’s really just... well, it's just the thought of work that casts a shadow over things. As long as I'm not thinking about that ridiculous new bilingual SEL curriculum or the mountain of unread emails sitting in my inbox, I'm perfectly capable of enjoying myself. The rest of my life is wonderful, it's just the school district that's making me so wound up.
Do you often find yourself criticizing yourself or feeling guilty about your performance as a teacher lately?

Guilty? Criticizing myself? Oh, no, not at all. I mean, I know I just spent all that time telling you how overwhelmed I am with the administrative side of things, but no, I don't feel guilty about my actual performance in the classroom. Why would I? 

Like I said before, I've been doing this for almost twenty-eight years. I know what good teaching looks like, and I know I'm still doing it. I mean, sure, maybe I'm not decorating my bulletin boards with quite the same Pinterest-level enthusiasm I had ten years ago, but the core of it—the actual instruction, the connection with the students—that's as strong as ever. 

Take my reading groups, for example. I have this one group of fifth graders this year who came to me reading at barely a third-grade level. They were so discouraged, and honestly, their previous teachers had kind of just passed them along because they were quiet kids who didn't cause trouble. But I didn't let them slide. I completely revamped my guided reading approach for them, brought in high-interest, lower-readability texts—mostly graphic novels and some really engaging nonfiction about extreme weather, which they just ate up—and we've been working on fluency and comprehension strategies every single day since September. And you know what? Two of those kids just tested at grade level on their spring assessments. Grade level! 

You don't get results like that if you're slacking off or doing a poor job. So no, I don't criticize my teaching. I know I'm doing everything I possibly can for those kids. The only thing I feel guilty about is that I can't give them even more of my time, because I'm constantly being pulled away to fill out some ridiculous online tracking form for the district's new initiative. 

It's the district that should feel guilty, honestly. They're the ones piling all these unrealistic expectations on us without any support. They're the ones who are failing the teachers, and by extension, the students. But me? No. I sleep perfectly fine at night knowing I'm doing right by my class. I just wish I could say the same for the people working at the central office.
Do you feel like you're a failure as a teacher because of the difficulties you're experiencing with the new curriculum?

A failure? Oh, heavens no. No, no, no. I mean, like I was just saying about my reading groups, I know exactly what I bring to the table. If anything, the only failure here is the rollout of this whole curriculum itself. 

I mean, you should see the pacing guide they handed us at the in-service back in August. It is completely, utterly detached from the reality of a modern classroom. They actually expect us to integrate these complex, high-level social-emotional prompts into the middle of a math block! I sat down with my grade-level team—Sarah and Michelle, who I’ve co-planned with for, oh, gosh, going on twelve years now—and we just looked at the giant binders they gave us and laughed. Well, it was a very tired laugh, but still. We know how ten-year-olds learn. We know that you can't just force a deep, reflective conversation about emotional regulation when you're in the middle of teaching long division. It just doesn't work that way. 

So when I inevitably fall behind on their impossible, pie-in-the-sky checklist, I don't look in the mirror and think, "Oh, I'm failing." Not for a single second. I have parents who specifically request me for their younger children because they saw how much their older kids thrived in my room. Just the other day, I got the sweetest email from a mother whose son I had three years ago, just checking in and saying how much he still talks about our class projects. You don't get messages like that if you're a failure. 

So, no, I certainly don't feel like a failure. The district might be failing us, and they are certainly failing the students with this administrative nonsense, but my conscience is completely clear on my end. I'm a very good teacher, and a bad curriculum doesn't change that.
Are there activities that you used to enjoy, but no longer find pleasure in?

No, no, I think I touched on this a bit earlier when we were talking about my garden and the crossword puzzles, but really, I haven't lost interest in anything at all. My outside life is completely intact. 

Like those historical fiction novels I mentioned earlier? Well, I've actually been in a neighborhood book club for... gosh, it has to be fifteen years now. We meet the third Thursday of every month, rain or shine, rotating houses. And I still look forward to it just as much as I did when we first started it. In fact, I hosted just last week. We were reading this new piece set in World War II—which is usually right up my alley, though honestly this particular one dragged a bit in the middle chapters—but anyway, I spent the whole afternoon before they came over making these little baked brie tartlets with raspberry preserves. I found the recipe in a magazine at the dentist's office and just had to try it. I got out the nice cloth napkins, made a big pot of decaf, and I just had such a wonderful time visiting with the ladies. 

And I still go to my water aerobics class at the YMCA on Tuesday and Thursday evenings, too. The instructor, Brenda, she’s been trying to get me to try the new Zumba class they're offering instead, but I always tell her, my knees just aren't what they used to be after standing on hard classroom floors for twenty-eight years, and the water is so much gentler! So I still go to my regular class, I still chat with the girls in the locker room, I still get a good workout in. 

So, really, no. Everything else in my life is just as enjoyable as it ever was. I haven't dropped a single hobby or stopped seeing my friends or lost my taste for cooking or anything like that. I actually just had my annual physical with my primary care doctor, Dr. Henderson, back in... oh, it must have been late February, right before the district dropped all this new administrative paperwork on us. And everything was absolutely pristine. My blood pressure is right where it should be—which is honestly a minor miracle considering what I have to deal with at work—and my cholesterol is fantastic, probably because I’m so diligent about packing those healthy lunches I told you about. 

And I still make sure to stay active, too. Teaching keeps you on your feet all day, of course, but beyond that, Tom and I always take our dog for a walk every single evening. We have a golden retriever mix named Barnaby, he's about six years old now, and he just has to get his energy out. So after we finish dinner and clean up the kitchen, we take him on this big loop around our subdivision. It takes about forty-five minutes, and we walk past the neighborhood park and down around the cul-de-sac... and I haven't missed a single night of that. Even when I’m dreading going into work the next day, I still get my walking shoes on. 

So, physically? I feel just as healthy and capable as I did ten years ago. No strange aches or pains, no fatigue during the day, nothing like that. My body is holding up beautifully. It really is just this mental and emotional exhaustion from the sheer volume of work they expect us to do without any support. But physically, no, I'm doing just fine.

doctor.question: Are you feeling pleasure or enjoyment from activities that you normally find pleasurable?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about anhedonia (loss of pleasure or enjoyment in activities), which is not part of my symptom profile for Adjustment Disorder.

patient.answer:
Pleasure? Oh, yes, absolutely. I haven't lost my joy for life or anything like that. I know sometimes when people get overwhelmed they just want to pull the covers up over their heads and sleep all weekend, but that is certainly not me. I still absolutely love my weekends and my hobbies. 

For instance, my garden. I have this perennial border along the back fence that I’ve been cultivating for... gosh, it must be five or six years now. And I still get just as much satisfaction out of it as I always have. Just this past Saturday, the weather was finally cooperating, so I spent a good three hours out there. The hostas are coming in beautifully this year, and I had to divide some of the daylilies—because if you don't stay on top of those, they will just completely take over the bed, they're practically weeds if you let them go—and I was just as happy as a clam with my gardening gloves on and my hands in the dirt. 

And Tom and I still have our Sunday morning routine, too. We always get the Sunday paper—the actual physical paper delivered to the driveway, which I know makes us absolute dinosaurs, but I just cannot do the crossword puzzle on an iPad, it is simply not the same without a real pen in your hand. We sit out on the sunporch with our coffee, and we tackle it together. He usually handles the sports and geography clues, and I do the literature and history ones. It’s honestly my favorite part of the week, and I still look forward to it just as much as I ever did. 

So, no, I'm definitely still enjoying the things I love. I still enjoy my garden, I still love taking Barnaby on those evening walks I mentioned, I still love reading my historical fiction novels before bed. It’s really just... well, it's just the thought of work that casts a shadow over things. As long as I'm not thinking about that ridiculous new bilingual SEL curriculum or the mountain of unread emails sitting in my inbox, I'm perfectly capable of enjoying myself. The rest of my life is wonderful, it's just the school district that's making me so wound up.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient is experiencing significant guilt or self-criticism
doctor.question: Do you often find yourself criticizing yourself or feeling guilty about your performance as a teacher lately?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feelings of guilt or excessive self-criticism, which are symptoms of depression (worthlessness/guilt). My symptom profile for Adjustment Disorder does not include this symptom.

patient.answer:
Guilty? Criticizing myself? Oh, no, not at all. I mean, I know I just spent all that time telling you how overwhelmed I am with the administrative side of things, but no, I don't feel guilty about my actual performance in the classroom. Why would I? 

Like I said before, I've been doing this for almost twenty-eight years. I know what good teaching looks like, and I know I'm still doing it. I mean, sure, maybe I'm not decorating my bulletin boards with quite the same Pinterest-level enthusiasm I had ten years ago, but the core of it—the actual instruction, the connection with the students—that's as strong as ever. 

Take my reading groups, for example. I have this one group of fifth graders this year who came to me reading at barely a third-grade level. They were so discouraged, and honestly, their previous teachers had kind of just passed them along because they were quiet kids who didn't cause trouble. But I didn't let them slide. I completely revamped my guided reading approach for them, brought in high-interest, lower-readability texts—mostly graphic novels and some really engaging nonfiction about extreme weather, which they just ate up—and we've been working on fluency and comprehension strategies every single day since September. And you know what? Two of those kids just tested at grade level on their spring assessments. Grade level! 

You don't get results like that if you're slacking off or doing a poor job. So no, I don't criticize my teaching. I know I'm doing everything I possibly can for those kids. The only thing I feel guilty about is that I can't give them even more of my time, because I'm constantly being pulled away to fill out some ridiculous online tracking form for the district's new initiative. 

It's the district that should feel guilty, honestly. They're the ones piling all these unrealistic expectations on us without any support. They're the ones who are failing the teachers, and by extension, the students. But me? No. I sleep perfectly fine at night knowing I'm doing right by my class. I just wish I could say the same for the people working at the central office.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's condition is impacting their self-esteem
doctor.question: Do you feel like you're a failure as a teacher because of the difficulties you're experiencing with the new curriculum?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feelings of worthlessness or feeling like a failure, which is a symptom of depression not covered in my Adjustment Disorder symptom profile.

patient.answer:
A failure? Oh, heavens no. No, no, no. I mean, like I was just saying about my reading groups, I know exactly what I bring to the table. If anything, the only failure here is the rollout of this whole curriculum itself. 

I mean, you should see the pacing guide they handed us at the in-service back in August. It is completely, utterly detached from the reality of a modern classroom. They actually expect us to integrate these complex, high-level social-emotional prompts into the middle of a math block! I sat down with my grade-level team—Sarah and Michelle, who I’ve co-planned with for, oh, gosh, going on twelve years now—and we just looked at the giant binders they gave us and laughed. Well, it was a very tired laugh, but still. We know how ten-year-olds learn. We know that you can't just force a deep, reflective conversation about emotional regulation when you're in the middle of teaching long division. It just doesn't work that way. 

So when I inevitably fall behind on their impossible, pie-in-the-sky checklist, I don't look in the mirror and think, "Oh, I'm failing." Not for a single second. I have parents who specifically request me for their younger children because they saw how much their older kids thrived in my room. Just the other day, I got the sweetest email from a mother whose son I had three years ago, just checking in and saying how much he still talks about our class projects. You don't get messages like that if you're a failure. 

So, no, I certainly don't feel like a failure. The district might be failing us, and they are certainly failing the students with this administrative nonsense, but my conscience is completely clear on my end. I'm a very good teacher, and a bad curriculum doesn't change that.

doctor.question: Are there activities that you used to enjoy, but no longer find pleasure in?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about anhedonia (loss of pleasure in previously enjoyed activities), which is not part of my symptom profile for Adjustment Disorder.

patient.answer:
No, no, I think I touched on this a bit earlier when we were talking about my garden and the crossword puzzles, but really, I haven't lost interest in anything at all. My outside life is completely intact. 

Like those historical fiction novels I mentioned earlier? Well, I've actually been in a neighborhood book club for... gosh, it has to be fifteen years now. We meet the third Thursday of every month, rain or shine, rotating houses. And I still look forward to it just as much as I did when we first started it. In fact, I hosted just last week. We were reading this new piece set in World War II—which is usually right up my alley, though honestly this particular one dragged a bit in the middle chapters—but anyway, I spent the whole afternoon before they came over making these little baked brie tartlets with raspberry preserves. I found the recipe in a magazine at the dentist's office and just had to try it. I got out the nice cloth napkins, made a big pot of decaf, and I just had such a wonderful time visiting with the ladies. 

And I still go to my water aerobics class at the YMCA on Tuesday and Thursday evenings, too. The instructor, Brenda, she’s been trying to get me to try the new Zumba class they're offering instead, but I always tell her, my knees just aren't what they used to be after standing on hard classroom floors for twenty-eight years, and the water is so much gentler! So I still go to my regular class, I still chat with the girls in the locker room, I still get a good workout in. 

So, really, no. Everything else in my life is just as enjoyable as it ever was. I haven't dropped a single hobby or stopped seeing my friends or lost my taste for cooking or anything like that. It's just the school stuff. I just want to go to work and teach my students without feeling like I'm drowning in district mandates, you know? But once I'm out of that building, I'm perfectly happy doing all my usual things.

patient.answer:
Weight? Oh, goodness, no. No, not at all. If anything, I might have put on a pound or two since the holidays, but certainly no significant weight loss. 

I mean, I've always been pretty consistent with my weight, give or take a little bit here and there. Like I mentioned, I still go to my water aerobics on Tuesdays and Thursdays, which helps keep me active. But honestly, with the way things have been at school lately, I've actually been baking more on the weekends. It’s sort of a stress relief for me, you know? Just last Sunday, after spending three hours trying to navigate that awful new grading portal the district forced on us, I just shut my laptop, went into the kitchen, and made a double batch of my grandmother’s snickerdoodles. The real ones, with the cream of tartar, not just sugar cookies rolled in cinnamon. 

And then, of course, there’s the book club I was telling you about. We always have snacks. I made those baked brie tartlets last week, and the month before that, when we were at Susan’s house, she made this incredible artichoke dip that I probably ate way too much of. We all did, really. 

Plus, my husband and I still do our regular Friday night pizza. We’ve been going to the same little Italian place down the street from us for—oh, it has to be over a decade now. We get the large thin crust with half pepperoni for him and half mushroom and green pepper for me, and we always split a house salad. It’s just our little end-of-the-week tradition, a way to decompress after I’ve spent Monday through Friday dealing with all that administrative red tape. 

So, no, my appetite hasn't changed one bit, and my clothes are fitting exactly the same as they always have. I haven't lost any weight. I’m eating perfectly fine. It’s just the stress from the school district that’s bothering me, not my appetite.
